subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Super-Earths
description: A quick, practical guide to Super-Earths.

hook.text: Super-Earths are planets between 1 and 10 Earth masses. Our solar system has none, but they're the most common type found.

buildup.text: They might be rocky like Earth or wrapped in thick hydrogen envelopes. We don't know for sure yet.

discovery.text: Kepler found that super-Earths are extremely common around other stars. Their absence here is the real mystery.

twist.text: Jupiter may have prevented super-Earths from forming in our solar system by disrupting their building materials early on.

climax.text: Some super-Earths sit in habitable zones. They're prime targets in the search for signs of life beyond Earth.

punchline.text: The galaxy's most common planet type. We don't have one. That's the puzzle.

quiz.question: What makes super-Earths unusual in the context of our solar system?
options: Our solar system has none, despite them being the most common planet type
They are the only planets known to have liquid water
They orbit farther from their stars than any planet in our system

details.summary: Super-Earths are exoplanets with masses between about 1.5 and 10 times Earth's — larger than our planet but smaller than Neptune. They're the most common type of planet in the galaxy yet absent from our solar system. Their compositions may range from rocky to water-rich to mini gas envelopes.
details.whyItMatters: Super-Earths are the galaxy's most common planet type, yet we have no local example to study. Understanding them is key to knowing what typical planets look like — and whether many could be habitable.
takeaways: The most common planet type in the galaxy
Absent from our own solar system

faq.question: Could super-Earths be habitable?
faq.answer: Potentially. Some in habitable zones could have liquid water, thicker atmospheres providing warmth, and stronger gravity retaining volatiles. However, thicker atmospheres might create greenhouse effects, and stronger gravity could limit plate tectonics.

faq.question: Why doesn't our solar system have a super-Earth?
faq.answer: Jupiter may be the reason. During the solar system's formation, Jupiter's migration may have disrupted the inner disk, preventing a super-Earth from forming. This 'Grand Tack' hypothesis explains the solar system's unusual architecture — most systems have super-Earths where we have a gap.
